Bangladesh improves in rule of law index but trails several African nations
item.description:
Bangladesh has made a slight improvement in its overall rule of law score but continues to rank below several African countries, including Kenya, Zimbabwe and Nigeria, according to the Rule of Law Index 2026 released on Wednesday.
Bangladesh ranked 123rd among 143 countries and jurisdictions in the World Justice Project (WJP) index, behind Zimbabwe (122nd), Nigeria (120th), Sierra Leone (110th), Liberia (103rd), Kenya (100th) and Ghana (62nd).
Its score increased by 0.6% to 0.393 out of 1, up from 0.391 in 2025, making Bangladesh the world's 15th-biggest improver and South Asia's top gainer. Its ranking improved by two places from 125th, although its score remained below the global average of 0.55.
The index assesses countries across eight factors: constraints on government powers, absence of corruption, open government, fundamental rights, order and security, regulatory enforcement, civil justice and criminal justice.
Bangladesh improved in only three factors — constraints on government powers, absence of corruption and regulatory enforcement — while its performance declined in the other five.
Fundamental rights remained the country's weakest area, with Bangladesh ranking 133rd and scoring 0.30, placing it among the 11 lowest-ranked countries.
The indicator assesses the protection of fundamental human rights under international law. Civil justice was the second-weakest area, with Bangladesh ranking 132nd and scoring 0.36. The indicator measures access to and the effectiveness of the civil justice system in resolving grievances.
Bangladesh ranked 124th in regulatory enforcement, with a score of 0.40, and 117th in criminal justice, scoring 0.32. In the absence of corruption category, which measures bribery, improper influence and the misappropriation of public resources, it ranked 113th with a score of 0.35.
The country ranked 111th in constraints on government powers, which measures accountability under the law, with a score of 0.38.
Open government was Bangladesh's highest-ranked factor at 106th, with a score of 0.41. It assesses government transparency, accountability mechanisms and public participation in policy deliberations.
Bangladesh ranked 107th in order and security, scoring 0.63. The factor measures how effectively a society protects individuals and property.
Despite the annual improvement, Bangladesh's overall rule of law score declined by 0.8% between 2021 and 2026, falling from 0.40 to around 0.39, according to the WJP's country profile.
Six of the index's eight factors deteriorated over the five-year period. Civil justice recorded the sharpest decline at 4.2%, followed by open government at 2.8%, fundamental rights at 1.5%, regulatory enforcement at 0.9%, criminal justice at 0.7% and absence of corruption at 0.2%.
Constraints on government powers and order and security improved by 2.3% and 0.6%, respectively.
Human rights activist and Supreme Court lawyer Barrister Jyotirmoy Barua attributed the deterioration partly to the worsening law and order situation.
"We had expected that an elected government would be able to turn things around to some extent, as the interim government had failed to maintain or restore control over the law and order situation," he said.
"However, the elected government has been trying to bring the entire situation under control at once, and the pressure associated with this has contributed to instability. Law enforcement is also closely linked to the justice system, and our overall performance in these areas has deteriorated," he added.
Nepal remained South Asia's top performer, ranking 71st globally with a score of 0.52, followed by Sri Lanka at 74th and India at 88th. Bangladesh ranked ahead of only Pakistan (131st) and Afghanistan (142nd) in the region.
Denmark topped the 2026 index, followed by Norway, Finland, Sweden and Luxembourg. Venezuela ranked last, preceded by Afghanistan, Haiti, Cambodia and Nicaragua.
The index drew on data from more than 215,000 households and 3,400 surveys of legal practitioners and experts across 143 countries and jurisdictions. The data were collected between February and August 2026.
The WJP highlighted the links between the rule of law and economic prosperity. Countries with GDP per capita above the global average of $14,406 scored at least 0.68 on the index, while those with inflation below the global median of 3.23% scored at least 0.60. The findings indicate an association between the rule of law, price stability and economic performance.

item.title: Nearly all coral reefs risk collapse in 50 years: IUCN
item.description:
FIJI-UN-COP31-CLIMATE-ENVIRONMENT

Nearly all of the world's shallow-water coral reefs face an "extremely high risk" of collapse by 2075 due to climate change, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) warned Thursday.

In the first global assessment of its kind, the world authority on threatened wildlife classified 96 percent of the planet's coral reef systems as "critically endangered" -- its highest risk category.

Corals are heat sensitive and particularly vulnerable to human-driven climate change, which is warming the world's oceans and increasing the frequency and intensity of damaging bleaching events.

"The risk of coral reef collapse is escalating, but this must be a wake-up call rather than a cause for despair," said Mishal Gudka, scientific lead of the IUCN Red List of Coral Reef Ecosystems assessment.

"Coral reefs have shown a remarkable ability to bounce back from devastating bleaching events," said Gudka, who is also research director at Coastal Oceans Research and Development in the Indian Ocean (CORDIO) East Africa, a conservation organisation.

For their assessment, researchers used the "middle-of-the-road" scenario from the UN's panel of climate experts that projects global temperatures rising 2.7C above pre-industrial levels by 2100.

The world is on track for 2.6C warming this century under current global commitments to cut planet-heating emissions, the United Nations warned Wednesday.

"Heat stress from climate change is the single most consistent threat driving coral reef decline worldwide," the IUCN said in a statement.

Overfishing is also hurting corals as certain herbivores and predators help control algae and maintain an ecological balance, the organisation said.

The overexploitation of parrotfish and other groupers threatens 63 percent of coral reef ecosystems.

Coastal development, pollution, tourism and more frequent storms are among other threats.

Critically endangered coral

The IUCN's analysis examined 127 tropical and subtropical coral systems covering 188,362 square kilometres.

The world's largest and most biodiverse coral reefs are among those classified as critically endangered -- Australia's Great Barrier Reef, the Coral Triangle in southeast Asia and the western Pacific, the Caribbean's Mesoamerican Barrier Reef System, and the Red Sea coral reefs.

A reef ecosystem collapses when hard corals -- which build its living foundation -- largely disappear and are replaced by algae, rubble and sponges.

The report was released during the UN's COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia, where governments are under pressure to make progress on a landmark pact to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030.

Despite its warning, the IUCN said coral reefs in most parts of the world "are not yet lost".

If scientists look only at what has happened over the past 50 years, excluding future climate projections, 24 percent of coral reef ecosystems would be deemed critically endangered instead of 96 percent, the IUCN said.

"It is not too late to give coral reefs a chance to recover, but it requires decisive action to tackle climate change and halt further ocean warming," said IUCN Director General Grethel Aguilar.

"We know what is needed: ambitious emissions reductions, stronger protection and restoration efforts, and sustained investment in resilient coastal ecosystems and the communities that depend on them."

A study published in the journal Nature last week found that, by 2020, nearly half of coral species were at "elevated relative risk of extinction", with climate change the main driver of this decline.

PHP security flaw triggers global cyber alert, millions of websites at risk
item.description:
Bangladesh e-Government Computer Incident Response Team (BGd e-GOV CIRT) has issued a high-severity alert over two critical security vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language widely used to build websites and web applications.
The vulnerabilities, collectively dubbed “PHP2Shell”, could allow hackers to remotely run malicious code on vulnerable servers without a username or password, potentially giving them control of affected systems.
The flaws, identified as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, carry a Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) score of 9.2 out of 10, placing them in the critical severity category.
According to the alert, the vulnerabilities stem from PHP’s memory management. Attackers could exploit situations involving memory exhaustion or data persisting from previous requests after memory is freed by sending specially crafted HTTP requests to gain control of a server.
Users of PHP-FPM and Apache’s mod_php are particularly at risk. Other potentially affected systems include PHP-CGI, FrankenPHP, LiteSpeed, Docker containers and shared hosting environments. Government portals, banks, e-commerce platforms and websites built on WordPress and Laravel could also be vulnerable.
A successful attack could result in full server compromise, data and file theft, exposure of database passwords and API keys, and website outages, the alert warned.
BGD e-GOV CIRT has urged administrators to update PHP immediately to the secure versions: 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. It also advised them to ensure that the server’s underlying PHP runtime is updated, not just the application framework.
For administrators unable to install the patches immediately, the agency recommended temporarily placing servers behind a VPN, restricting access through IP-based allowlists and increasing log monitoring.
However, BGD e-GOV CIRT stressed that updating PHP is the only permanent solution.

Dhaka, Tokyo eye multiple MoUs during PM’s Japan visit
item.description:
Bangladesh and Japan expect to sign more than four memorandums of understanding (MoUs) during Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s upcoming visit to Japan and issue a joint statement outlining the outcomes and future direction of bilateral cooperation. The proposed documents seek to expand cooperation in agriculture, fisheries, human resource development, skills enhancement, civil aviation, trade, environmental conservation and local government modernization. The prime minister will undertake the four-day official visit from October 26 to 29 at the invitation of his Japanese counterpart Sanae Takaichi.
Preparations are underway on around eight cooperation documents. The final number to be signed, however, will depend on the completion of negotiations between the two sides. “We hope that many of these MoUs will be signed during the visit,” Foreign Secretary Asad Alam Siam said. The anticipated joint statement is expected to set out the outcomes of the bilateral talks and priorities for advancing the Bangladesh-Japan strategic partnership. Former Dhaka University Vice-Chancellor Prof Dr Anwarullah Chowdhury said the proposed agreements could broaden the relationship by connecting Bangladesh’s development priorities with Japan’s industrial experience, technology and institutional expertise. “Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s visit offers an important opportunity to give fresh momentum to our longstanding partnership with Japan. The proposed MoUs can create a stronger basis for cooperation in sectors closely linked to production, employment and people’s livelihoods,” he said. Chowdhury said cooperation in agriculture and fisheries should focus on productivity, processing, preservation and quality management, while skills programs should reflect employers’ needs. “Language teaching and technical training should advance together. Our objective should be to prepare workers for better employment opportunities while also developing the skilled workforce needed by industries in Bangladesh,” he said. He stressed the importance of involving local enterprises in Japanese investment initiatives to extend the benefits to domestic suppliers and smaller businesses. “Alongside large investments, we should encourage partnerships between Japanese medium-sized companies and Bangladeshi entrepreneurs. Such cooperation can help our businesses improve production methods, quality control and management,” he said. The former vice-chancellor suggested preparing an implementation plan after the visit, identifying responsible agencies, deadlines and arrangements for reviewing progress. “Signing an MoU is an important beginning. Its lasting value will depend on the investment, jobs, skills and institutional capabilities that follow,” he said. Under the announced program, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman will hold high-level bilateral talks with his Japanese counterpart Takaichi at her office on October 27. The two leaders will lead their respective delegations in the official talks. The Japanese premier will also host a luncheon in honor of the Bangladesh Prime Minister. Tarique Rahman is scheduled to deliver the keynote address at the Japan-Bangladesh Economic Forum and meet Japanese business leaders to discuss investment opportunities and commercial partnerships. His tentative program includes meetings with the Japan-Bangladesh Parliamentary Friendship League and the chairman of the Japan-Bangladesh Committee for Commercial and Economic Cooperation. Meetings are also being planned with the president of the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA), the governor of the Japan Bank for International Cooperation (JBIC) and the president of the Japan External Trade Organization (JETRO). An engagement with the chairman of the Sasakawa Peace Foundation is also under consideration. The proposed itinerary includes visits to an LNG terminal and power plant in Chiba and a Toyota factory in Nagoya.
The prime minister will be accompanied by his spouse Dr Zubaida Rahman, ministers, advisers, senior officials and other delegation members. The delegation will travel on Biman Bangladesh Airlines flights. Beyond the signing program, the visit offers an opportunity to advance the implementation of the Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA), signed on February 6 this year, and address practical requirements for expanding trade and investment. Siam said discussions would focus on implementing the agreement, widening access for Bangladeshi products to the Japanese market and strengthening business engagement. Infrastructure costs and financing terms will also feature in the talks amid an 83 per cent increase in the cost of Dhaka’s MRT Line-1 and a 113 per cent rise in that of MRT Line-5. Asked whether the cost increases and lower interest rates on Japanese loans would be discussed, Siam said Bangladesh had sought financing and technical assistance for infrastructure development. “These infrastructure cooperation issues will certainly come up during the bilateral meeting between the two prime ministers,” he said, adding that discussions would extend beyond metro rail. “We want to obtain loans at lower interest rates from all countries,” he said, noting that global financing arrangements and country-specific factors would influence the outcome. Japan supports major projects in Bangladesh, including the metro rail, Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport’s Third Terminal and infrastructure development in Matarbari. The Bay of Bengal Industrial Growth Belt, or BIG-B, initiative, launched in 2014, provides a framework linking infrastructure, industry and regional connectivity. Prof Chowdhury said Matarbari and Araihazar offered opportunities to connect infrastructure investment with industrial production, local suppliers and employment. “Prepared land, reliable electricity and water, transport connections and predictable approval procedures will help turn investor interest into operating businesses,” he added. Renewable energy, science and technology, digital transformation and human resource development will also feature in the discussions, the foreign secretary said. Beyond bilateral matters, the two sides will discuss regional and international peace and stability, cooperation in addressing the energy crisis and a sustainable, peaceful solution to the Rohingya crisis. The visit will seek to build on that longstanding relationship through new cooperation instruments, stronger institutional engagement and expanded economic opportunities.

item.title: Russia, Ukraine agree on ceasefire in Oleshky from 27 Oct, to hold peace talks next month
item.description:
UKRAINE-CRISIS/OLESHKY

Ukraine and Russia said on Friday they had agreed on a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky, brokered through US first lady Melania Trump, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said peace negotiators would meet next month for new talks.

The two sides said the ceasefire would go into effect on 27 October, allowing the delivery of aid and the evacuation of residents through humanitarian corridors.

Amid a US push to organise new talks aimed at ending the 4-1/2-year-old war, Zelenskiy said negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the United States had agreed to technical-level meetings in the first half of November in Abu Dhabi. A US official later said the three countries may hold their next talks in a couple weeks in Abu Dhabi or Switzerland.

Zelenskiy said he hoped a meeting of the countries' leaders would follow.

Previous rounds of talks headed by the United States stalled in February ⁠with no significant progress towards ending the bloodiest conflict in Europe since World War Two. Russia continues to demand Ukraine cede all of the eastern Donbas region, including territory Russia has not occupied militarily, while Kyiv rejects any notion of giving up land it currently holds.

The latest peace efforts follow a rift between Washington and Kyiv in recent weeks and a series of moves by US President Donald Trump seen as favouring Russia.

A major source of friction was limitations placed on SpaceX's Starlink communication system that Ukraine uses to protect against incoming attacks. Trump said on Friday that if Ukraine still faced a problem with the system, he would straighten it out and, if necessary, speak about the matter to SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.

Another contentious point was Trump's announcement of a deal to allow Russia to provide diesel for the US and global markets, an agreement denounced by Ukraine and meant to keep prices down as the president's Republicans contest US midterm elections.

On Friday, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said the first three tankers with Russian diesel were on their way to North America.

In the town of Oleshky, occupied by Russian forces since February 2022, residents have reported that they faced a deepening food crisis.

"Both nations agreed to temporarily stop all military action in Oleshky to allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway," the White House said in a statement.

The chief of staff of Russian forces, Valery Gerasimov, said on the Defence Ministry's Telegram channel that Russian troops would halt fire from 4 a.m. local time (0100 GMT) on October 27 to allow for the humanitarian operation to start.

Ukraine's General Staff issued a statement agreeing to observe the ceasefire from the same time and pledging to "do everything possible to help Oleshky's residents." Ukraine says it has already used drones twice to send food into the town.

Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, also said the ceasefire would go into effect on October 27 and told Reuters the operation would involve demining roads to the town, deliveries of food and evacuations of civilians.

Melania trump's diplomatic efforts

Both sides said Melania Trump played an important role in coordinating the agreement. The first lady has been active in trying to get Ukrainian children seized by Russia during the war returned to their families.

"Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster," she said in a statement.

"Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food and clean water."

Pope Leo had spoken in the past week both to Zelenskiy and to Russian President Vladimir Putin about conditions in Oleshky.

The White House said Oleshky, located across the Dnipro River from the Ukrainian-held city of Kherson, had 1,700 to 2,000 residents remaining, down from 24,000 before the war.

US envoys

Zelenskiy's comments on resuming peace talks followed a meeting with US presidential envoy Steve Witkoff in Norway early this week and a subsequent meeting between Witkoff and Putin in St Petersburg.

Zelenskiy said he spoke on Friday with Witkoff and US envoy Jared Kushner. He said any peace agreement would need strong security guarantees for Ukraine and funding for 10 years to maintain the Ukrainian army.

"The plan is to meet in the first half of November, and as early as possible, of course," Zelenskiy told the Hudson Institute think tank via a video link. He said much would depend on Russia, noting that a similar meeting expected this month had not materialised.

Zelenskiy spoke of the importance of continued diplomatic efforts to reach a ceasefire and end the war, now in its fifth year, adding that Europe should also be involved in the talks.

Ukrainian officials said on Friday that speed restrictions on Starlink systems in Ukraine remained in place, despite Trump's previous statement that the services had been fully restored.

Trump told reporters at the White House on Friday that he had not spoken to Musk about the restrictions but would do so if required.

"If there is a problem, I'll get it straightened out," he said. The caps have been in place since October 13.

Ukraine and Russia also swapped 270 servicemen each in a prisoner exchange on Friday, the Russian Defence Ministry said. Zelenskiy described the swap, the first since August, as a "very important result."

Ukraine's acting prosecutor, Anton Kovalskyi, writing on Telegram, said more than 19,000 Ukrainian civilians, including 762 children, had been killed since Russia launched its full-scale war more than four years ago.

item.title: PHP flaws: Bangladesh Bank, land services, six banks’ websites remain offline
item.description:
CYBERSECURITY-PHP/

The websites of Bangladesh Bank, the land services department and six banks remain offline due to a security vulnerability identified in PHP, a widely used programming language for website development.

The websites have been temporarily taken down to avoid potential cyber risks and assess the security of their technological infrastructure. The websites were found offline at around 11:00am on Saturday.

PHP flaws prompt millions of hacking attempts amid rush to patch vulnerabilities

Bangladesh Bank has kept its website offline since Thursday. Following the central bank's move, several other banks also shut down their websites as a precautionary measure. The banks are Agrani Bank, Janata Bank, IFIC Bank, Standard Islami Bank, SBAC Bank and Bengal Commercial Bank.

The banks concerned said the measure had been taken to avoid potential cyber risks and assess the security of their technological infrastructure. The websites will be restored once the security assessments and necessary measures are completed.

Meanwhile, in response to the PHP security vulnerability, the Ministry of Land has also taken its digital land services website offline for maintenance.

Websites shut down worldwide amid fears of cyberattacks: How prepared is Bangladesh?

According to an announcement by the ministry, the maintenance work is scheduled to continue for 36 hours, from midnight between Thursday and Friday until noon on Saturday. During this period, land services will not be available through the website land.gov.bd.

On 22 October, the government's cyber security agency, BGD e-GOV CIRT, issued an urgent alert regarding the PHP security vulnerability. It advised relevant organisations to identify the use of PHP on their servers, check whether the versions in use were vulnerable and take necessary security measures.

PHP is a widely used programming language for developing websites and web applications. Security vulnerabilities in PHP can put the security of related software and servers at risk. As a precaution, various organisations are assessing the security of their websites and technological infrastructure.

item.title: Bangladesh's denim exports to EU rise 12.71pc in August
item.description:
Bangladesh's denim exports to the European Union grew 12.71 per cent year-on-year in August 2026 to 134.08 million euros, from 118.96 million euros a year earlier, according to Eurostat data.

The August growth outpaced the overall market, as total EU denim imports from the world rose 11.23 per cent to 430.16 million euros. Bangladesh's share of the EU's August imports stood at about 31.2 per cent, up from about 30.8 per cent a year earlier.

Over January-August, however, Bangladesh's shipments fell 5.85 per cent to 869.13 million euros from 923.11 million euros, a drop of about 54 million euros. The decline was sharper than the overall market's 4.40 per cent fall to 2,956.21 million euros.

As a result, Bangladesh's eight-month market share slipped to 29.40 per cent from about 29.9 per cent a year earlier. It nonetheless remained the EU's largest denim supplier, well ahead of Pakistan, by about 344 million euros.

Pakistan, the second-largest supplier, saw August exports grow 14.99 per cent to 87.71 million euros, but its January-August shipments fell 7.88 per cent to 525.49 million euros, a 17.78 per cent share.

Turkey, the third-largest, was hit hardest. Its August exports fell 13.26 per cent to 58.84 million euros, and its eight-month exports dropped 21.08 per cent to 438.25 million euros, a 14.82 per cent share.

Tunisia's eight-month exports fell 6.44 per cent to 219.94 million euros, while Cambodia's declined 6.47 per cent to 144.83 million euros. Morocco fell 14.48 per cent to 63.87 million euros.

Egypt was the standout, with exports up 59.57 per cent in August to 30.67 million euros and up 31.46 per cent over eight months to 188.14 million euros, for a 6.36 per cent share. China's exports rose 17.70 per cent over eight months to 197.13 million euros, giving it a 6.67 per cent share.

Vietnam and India, though small, posted strong growth. Vietnam's eight-month exports rose 45.38 per cent to 53.98 million euros, and India's rose 18.62 per cent to 31.40 million euros.

Bangladesh's eight-month decline was milder than that of Pakistan, Turkey, Tunisia, Cambodia and Morocco.

Talking to BSS, former Director of BGMEA Mohiuddin Rubel said Bangladesh has maintained a strong position in the European Union (EU) denim market despite an overall decline in apparel imports, thanks to its well-established supply chain, skilled workforce and technological capabilities.

He said Bangladesh had developed a strong foundation in denim manufacturing over many years, enabling the country to remain competitive in major markets, including Europe and the United States.

“Bangladesh has a strong supply chain base that has developed over many years. We have built expertise in technicians, technology and other areas of production,” Rubel said.

He said the country could further strengthen its position by shifting from volume-based production towards higher-value products, expanding value addition and adopting innovative technologies.

Although Bangladesh does not produce cotton, its strong fabric manufacturing capacity and established industrial base provide significant opportunities to upgrade denim products and increase export earnings, he added.

Rubel said the current slowdown in the European apparel market had affected exporters across countries, largely due to inflation, weaker imports and energy-related challenges.

Despite the difficult market conditions, Bangladesh continued to hold the leading position in the EU denim segment, with a substantial gap between the country and its nearest competitor, he said.

Rubel also stressed the importance of preparing for evolving EU trade rules, Generalised Scheme of Preferences (GSP) requirements and the European Green Deal.

Bangladesh should therefore focus on higher-value products, technological upgrading, innovation and compliance with emerging sustainability requirements to sustain its long-term growth in the global denim industry, he added.

item.title: Humaiun: Bangladesh reaffirms commitment to multilateralism, UN reform
item.description:
Bangladesh remains firmly committed to multilateralism and supports meaningful UN reform to address global challenges State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir said in a message marking United Nations Day, on Saturday.
He said the government, under Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s leadership, remained determined to strengthen democratic governance, uphold human rights and the rule of law, and promote accountable institutions.
The election of Bangladesh’s foreign minister as president of the 81st UN General Assembly underscored the government’s renewed impetus for multilateral engagement, he said.
Kobir said Bangladesh supported a more representative, transparent and effective UN, including meaningful reform of the Security Council, so that the organization could respond to contemporary realities and deliver for all.
“At a time of growing geopolitical tensions, armed conflicts, humanitarian crises and widening inequalities, multilateralism is not merely an option, it is an imperative,” he said.
He called for renewed commitment to dialogue, peaceful settlement of disputes, sovereign equality and respect for international law.
Highlighting Bangladesh’s contribution to global peace, the state minister said the country’s engagement with the UN was rooted in action and solidarity.
As one of the leading contributors to UN peacekeeping operations, Bangladesh’s peacekeepers continued to serve in challenging environments worldwide, he said.
He reaffirmed Bangladesh’s commitment to advancing women’s participation in peacekeeping and decision-making on peace and security.
Kobir said Bangladesh’s partnership with the UN extended to sustainable development, disaster resilience, poverty reduction, gender equality and humanitarian action.
Noting that Bangladesh continued to host more than 1.2 million Rohingyas forcibly displaced from Myanmar, he called for sustained international support for their early and sustainable return to Myanmar.
He also stressed the need to ensure finance, technology and capacity-building support for developing countries, least developed countries and climate-vulnerable nations as the international community pursued the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.
Extending warm greetings to the UN and its member states, Kobir said United Nations Day highlighted the enduring relevance of the UN Charter and collective action in addressing shared global challenges.
“Let us work together to restore trust, bridge divisions and build a world where peace, justice and prosperity are shared by all,” he said.

item.title: IGP: Police may initiate extortion cases on digital evidence alone
item.description:
Police will be empowered to file cases against extortionists on their own initiative, without requiring public complaints, under a proposed new law, Inspector General of Police (IGP) Ali Hossain Fakir has said.
The proposed law will allow police to take action against suspected extortionists based on digital evidence or information from other sources, he said.
“Extortionists are either criminals or connected to people in positions of power. As a result, people are often afraid to testify against them or lodge complaints with police,” the IGP said.
He made the remarks while responding to questions from journalists after a community policing meeting at Khulna Metropolitan Police Lines on Saturday afternoon.
Fakir said he had proposed to the home minister that a new law be enacted to strengthen action against extortion.
“Under the proposed law, police will be able to file cases and take action on their own initiative without requiring complaints from the public. If evidence, including digital evidence, is found, appropriate action can be taken against the accused. You will see a new law being introduced in the coming days,” he said.
The IGP said the initiative was aimed at eliminating extortion from society.
On rebuilding public trust in police, Fakir acknowledged that the force had become distanced from the public due to its activities over the past 17 years. He said his visit to Khulna was aimed at restoring public confidence and working to establish peace.
“Joint operations are underway against drugs, juvenile gangs, criminals and extortionists,” he said, adding that a legal framework was being developed with approval from the ministries of home affairs and finance to make police operations more effective.
He also said community policing would operate as a dedicated branch of the police force.
On the law and order situation in Khulna, the IGP said violence involving criminals had created fear among the public, with some criminals being killed and others committing murders.
“When police enforce the law, some demand the use of force. If force is used, they call the police fascist; if it is not used, they call the police weak. We do not want this,” he said.
He called for collective efforts to establish peace and justice and eliminate corruption through an effective police force.
Asked about the deterioration of law and order, Fakir recalled the situation after August 5, 2024, saying police had been absent from many areas and criminal activities had been widespread.
“Police have now regained their morale and resumed operations across the country. Not every problem can be resolved overnight, but the situation has improved,” he said.
The IGP said police wanted to become more humane and public-friendly, although some people argued that criminals no longer feared law enforcers.
He noted that some offenders resumed criminal activities shortly after being brought to justice, adding that police were developing policies to prevent repeat offences.
Fakir also said drugs had become entrenched in society over the past 17 years and that the current government had adopted a zero-tolerance policy towards narcotics.

item.title: Russia, Ukraine agree to US-brokered, 1 city ceasefire
item.description:
US first lady Melania Trump helped broker a ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia in the city of Oleshky, the White House announced Friday. The localized truce, according to the White House, is slated to begin on October 29.
The Ukrainian city occupied by Russia on the frontline of the war faces a humanitarian crisis and only around 2,000 people still live there. Prior to the war, the city had a population of around 24,000.
Oleshky has been under blockade since 2025 and was first occupied when Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
The city is located in southern Ukraine, just 9 kilometers (around 5.6 miles) from the major city of Kherson.
“Oleshky’s remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food and clean water,” Melania Trump said in a statement. “The people of Oleshky have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks.”
Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, thanked the first lady for securing the deal.
“Under our agreement: first a ceasefire will be put in place; second, humanitarian aid will be delivered to Oleshky; and third, civilians will be allowed to move freely out of Oleshky,” Lubinets said in a video message posted on Telegram. “The operation will be carried out gradually and is extremely challenging to implement.”
Russia also confirmed the agreement and said it will halt fire earlier than what the White House announced at 0400 local time (0100 GMT) on October 27.
According to the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights, residents in Oleshky say Russian occupying forces prevented them from leaving the city. Oleshky residents also say Russia has used civilians to shield military positions in the city — a war crime under international humanitarian law.
The ceasefire deal in Oleshky comes as US, Ukrainian and Russian negotiators are expected to meet in Abu Dhabi next month to discuss ending the war.
“The plan is to meet in the first half of November, and as early as possible, of course,” Zelensky told the US conservative Hudson Institute think tank.
In comments to Russian state news outlet TASS, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov also said preparations are underway for a three-way meeting in mid-November. Russian President Vladimir Putin said security would be a main topic for the Abu Dhabi talks.
“That is the security of both countries, Russia and Ukraine, after there has been a transition to a peace settlement,” Peskov said.
The Kremlin spokesperson said Russia only sees the Europeans at the table during a later stage in the talks. European leaders such as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz have said Europe must be involved in future Ukraine peace talks.
“It is clear that the architecture of European security cannot be discussed without other participants,” Peskov added.
US President Donald Trump has grown increasingly frustrated at Zelensky, and is pressuring him to “make a deal.”
Trump has blamed Ukraine for rising diesel prices in the US, as the US-Israeli war against Iran has caused the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and drove up the cost of gas at the pump for American consumers.
Trump has backed a deal to buy diesel from Russia to lower prices at fuel pumps, drawing criticism from Ukraine. The Kremlin said Friday that the first tanker of Russian diesel has set sail for the US despite the backlash from Ukraine.
Most recently, there has been controversy that tech billionaire Elon Musk ordered a slowdown of the Starshield military communications system that Ukraine relies on, possibly with the backing of Trump.
Trump has denied that he ordered restrictions on Starlink. He also defended Musk in comments to reporters on Friday and said, “Elon will never do anything wrong.”
“You know, whether I called or whether somebody else called, doesn’t make any difference,” Trump said. “I guess the bottom line, he put it back.”
Meanwhile, Zelensky and Ukraine said Friday that the system was still being throttled in Ukraine.
“It works, but it’s still limited,” Zelensky told US broadcaster ABC News.
A source in Ukraine’s Defense Ministry told AFP news agency and other news outlets that Ukrainians were witnessing “instances of signal loss” when using Starshield.
“There is currently no confirmation that the restrictions have been lifted,” the source added.

Bangladesh asks Saudi Arabia 6 questions over execution of 2 citizens
item.description:
Bangladesh has sent a diplomatic letter to Saudi Arabia seeking detailed information about the crimes committed by two Bangladeshi citizens executed in Mecca, how their sentences were carried out, where their bodies are now, and whether they had lawyers during their trials.

The questions were raised in a diplomatic letter sent by the Bangladesh Consulate General in Jeddah to the Mecca branch of Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs on 19 October.

Several senior officials at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed the information to Prothom Alo on Friday. They said Bangladesh’s Consul General in Jeddah, Md Sakhawat Hossain, met Farid bin Saad Al Shehri, director general of the Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs, in Jeddah on 19 October. He handed over the diplomatic letter during the meeting.

Around 7,500 Bangladeshis in Saudi prisons; government seeks copies of death sentences against two citizens

Reportedly, Bangladeshi citizens Nazrul Islam Abdul Bashir and Sweety Akter were executed in the Mecca region on 14 October. The death sentences were imposed as discretionary punishments by a judge. In this connection, the consulate has requested information on six specific points and asked for a response as soon as possible.

In the letter to the Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Bangladesh raised six questions about the execution of its two citizens. These include the type and nature of the offences; when and where they took place; when the two were arrested; a copy of the verdict against the two Bangladeshi nationals certified by respective authority; and how the death sentences were carried out—whether they were publicly executed by beheading with a sword or by another method.

Bangladesh has also asked where the bodies are being kept following the executions and whether they will be sent to Bangladesh or have already been buried in Saudi Arabia. It has further asked whether lawyers were appointed to represent the two accused during the investigation and trial, and whether either of them had requested legal assistance.

20 more Bangladeshis on Saudi convict list, sentences undisclosed

According to sources familiar with the matter in Dhaka, neither the Bangladesh mission in Dhaka nor the one in Jeddah has detailed information about the entire process leading to the executions. In particular, the missions are unable to confirm whether the two men had legal representation during their trials.

Diplomatic sources said Saudi authorities regularly provide Bangladesh with lists of Bangladeshi nationals who are imprisoned or have been convicted. Those two were named on the September list. One was accused of “adultery” and the other of an “ICT”, or information technology-related, offence. However, the list did not specify their sentences. As a result, Bangladesh was unable to provide them with consular services without knowing that they had been sentenced to death.

According to a statement by the Saudi interior ministry, they were sentenced for violating the sanctity of a mosque complex in Mecca by engaging in indecent acts. It remains unclear how the allegations listed in the document correspond to the ministry’s statement. The consulate’s first question, therefore, is not merely an attempt to obtain information, but also to clarify the discrepancy.

Bangladeshis among 59 foreigners executed in Saudi Arabia in first 6 months

Questions raised in high-level talks

At a meeting on 19 October, Bangladesh’s consul general in Jeddah asked Farid bin Saad Al Shehri, director general of the Saudi foreign ministry, why the information had been incomplete. According to diplomatic sources, had the mission known about the death sentences, it could have taken steps to protect the two citizens. In such cases, efforts are generally made to provide legal assistance, pursue appeals and seek high-level diplomatic intervention.

Last week, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir told journalists in Dhaka that the execution of two Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia following allegations of criminal offences is a matter of disappointment for Bangladesh. According to information received from Saudi Arabia, the sentences were carried out this month after trials in lower and appellate courts.

A foreign ministry official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Saudi Arabia had sent a list of around 2,500 prisoners on 30 September. The list stated that 22 Bangladeshis had been sentenced, including the two who were executed, but did not specify the exact nature of the sentences. Bangladesh has therefore written to Saudi Arabia seeking specific information about those other 20 individuals.

Several foreign ministry officials told Prothom Alo that Saudi authorities had yet to respond to the diplomatic note. The officials are waiting for a reply.

item.title: Rooppur unit 1 clears B-2 tests, moves closer to power generation
item.description:
The first unit of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant has moved a step closer to electricity generation after successfully completing its B-2 phase physics tests and other required technical tests.
Detailed reports on the tests have been submitted to the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority (BAERA) for review.
Dr Md Zahedul Hasan, managing director of the Nuclear Power Plant Company Bangladesh Ltd (NPCBL), said on Saturday that the unit would enter the “C stage”, or power startup phase, once it receives final approval from the regulator.
The progress was also reported to the ministry at a recent meeting with a Russian delegation, he said.
Project sources said power startup is targeted for the end of October, subject to BAERA’s approval. Generation will initially begin at a low level and gradually increase.
The unit is expected to start supplying electricity to the national grid once it reaches 25–30% of its capacity. At least 300MW could be added to the grid by the end of this year, according to the project timeline.
The start of commercial operations will mark a major milestone for Bangladesh, strengthening its energy security and technological capabilities while bringing the country into the ranks of nuclear power-producing nations.
Built by Rosatom’s Atomstroyexport division, the plant will have two Generation III+ VVER-1200 reactors with a combined capacity of 2,400MW.
The project deadline has been extended to June 2028, while the estimated cost has risen to Tk138,686 crore due to the depreciation of the taka against the US dollar.

item.title: Cybersecurity threat spreads worldwide, affecting Bangladesh too
item.description:
Around 300,000 people in Bangladesh use online services to register changes in land ownership, known as mutation, every month. But when people tried to access the e-mutation service yesterday, Saturday, they found it unavailable.

The government website land.gov.bd, which provides the mutation service, said it was being updated as part of an urgent cybersecurity alert issued by BGD e-GOV CIRT. As a result, land services were temporarily suspended.

Sources at BGD e-GOV CIRT, the agency responsible for overseeing cybersecurity for the government, said the alert had been issued after a security vulnerability in PHP was discovered worldwide.

The vulnerability has led to websites being taken offline around the world. Several websites in Bangladesh have also been temporarily shut down. Besides the land services website, these include Bangladesh Bank, several public and private banks, a private hospital and websites operated by other organisations.

Bangladesh Bank website restored after 3-day shutdown over cyberattack fears

The organisations have taken their websites offline to strengthen security. CIRT sources, however, said they had identified at least one hospital website that had been compromised.

None of the organisations has publicly acknowledged that its website was taken offline because of the PHP vulnerability, making it difficult to establish how many institutions in Bangladesh have been affected.

Asif Mahmud, deputy project director of the Land Management Automation Project, was asked whether the land services website had been taken offline because of the PHP vulnerability.

He told Prothom Alo that a technical issue was being checked in coordination with the Bangladesh Computer Council (BCC) as part of routine maintenance. The website had been taken offline temporarily for this purpose, he said.

He added that the site was scheduled to remain unavailable until noon on Sunday, but it would be restored earlier if the work was completed before then.

The notice on the website, however, says it is being updated in response to an urgent cybersecurity alert from BGD e-GOV CIRT.

What is PHP and why did it take government websites offline?

What is PHP?

Many internet users may never have heard of PHP, yet they interact with it regularly. PHP, short for “PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor”, is a programming language that operates in the background, on the back end of websites.

A BBC report published on Friday, citing cybersecurity firm Wiz, said PHP powers around 70 per cent of websites worldwide. It was developed in the 1990s by Canadian programmer Rasmus Lerdorf, who made its source code publicly available. This allowed anyone to use it free of charge and modify it as needed.

The BBC report offered an example to explain how PHP works. Imagine ordering a burger at a restaurant. The server takes your order to the kitchen, where the burger is prepared and then brought to your table.

A website works in a similar way. When someone visits a website, PHP processes the request and generates the webpage accordingly. This happens almost instantly in the background, without the user noticing.

PHP flaws prompt 12-hour shutdown of digital land services server

How was the vulnerability discovered?

The PHP vulnerability had existed for more than a decade without being detected. Last week, a team of researchers from two US cybersecurity companies identified it with the help of artificial intelligence (AI). The companies are Calif and Wiz, the latter being part of Alphabet, Google’s parent company.

Ryan Austin, a researcher at Calif who helped identify the flaw, told the BBC that it was the most serious vulnerability he had ever discovered.

Concern spread worldwide after news of the vulnerability became public. Fearing that hackers would exploit it to take control of websites and steal data, organisations began announcing precautionary shutdowns.

PHP flaws prompt millions of hacking attempts amid rush to patch vulnerabilities

What has been the impact?

On 21 October, the US National Security Agency (NSA) warned all organisations using PHP. It said that if an organisation could not promptly fix the vulnerability, it should shut down the affected systems. The flaw could allow attackers to target databases directly.

According to the BBC, the alert disrupted various online services, including gaming platforms, government websites and online forums. Among the affected organisations was Wikimedia, the US-based non-profit that operates Wikipedia. As a precaution, it shut down several of its systems.

The UK government said on Thursday that some of its services might remain temporarily unavailable. It had shut down 32 websites as a precaution.

French telecommunications company Orange said it had restricted access to certain services worldwide while work to fix the vulnerability was under way. The Finnish government also took some websites and webpages offline. Some BBC pages were temporarily unavailable as well. The Dutch cybersecurity agency shut down its own website.

Amid the global disruption, a hacking group called “Siriusim” claimed to have gained access to confidential customer information at India’s State Bank of India (SBI), the country’s largest bank. On Friday, the state-owned bank acknowledged that customer data had been leaked.

Although hundreds of websites have reportedly been taken offline worldwide, no organisation has yet disclosed the total financial losses. Nor has the overall number of affected websites been confirmed. Guidance has been issued on how to improve security, including updating PHP to reduce the risk.

PHP flaws: Bangladesh Bank, land services, six banks’ websites remain offline

Websites shut down in Bangladesh

BGD e-GOV CIRT issued an urgent alert concerning PHP on Thursday, 22 October. It advised relevant organisations to identify PHP installations on their servers, check whether the versions in use were vulnerable and take the necessary security measures.

Bangladesh Bank took its website offline on Thursday following the alert. After the central bank’s move, several other banks also shut down their websites as a precaution. They include Agrani Bank, Janata Bank, IFIC Bank, Standard Islami Bank, SBAC Bank and Bengal Commercial Bank.

The banks said the measures were intended to avoid potential cyber risks and assess the security of their technology infrastructure. Their websites would be restored once the security checks and necessary measures had been completed.

Arif Hossain Khan, executive director and spokesperson for Bangladesh Bank, told Prothom Alo yesterday, “The website has been taken offline as a precaution. Officials from our technology department are working around the clock to ensure that no problems arise. Banking services have not been affected. The website will be restored once the risk has been reduced.”

BGD e-GOV CIRT sources said they had so far identified a private hospital website in Bangladesh as having been compromised. Although the hospital authorities had been informed, they had not contacted CIRT by Saturday evening. Maintenance work was under way on other government and private-sector websites that use PHP.

Nazmul Haque Khandoker, project director of CIRT, told Prothom Alo that after issuing an advisory on the PHP-related problem, the agency had notified organisations whose websites are hosted at the National Data Centre, as well as those covered by the National Portal Framework.

It had also alerted organisations designated as critical information infrastructure (CII). All organisations whose websites are built using PHP had been advised to take the necessary measures, he said.

Websites shut down worldwide amid fears of cyberattacks: How prepared is Bangladesh?

‘Definitely a cause for concern’

Leaks of citizens’ personal information have become commonplace in Bangladesh. A report published in August by the technology research organisation TechGlobal Institute (TGI) said at least 68 data breaches had occurred in the country between January 2023 and May 2026. Of these, 36 involved government organisations and 32 involved private entities.

In February last year, data from the national identity card (NID) database was leaked. In 2023, information belonging to 50 million people was also exposed in an NID data breach. No action was taken in response to these incidents, the report said.

Against this backdrop, BM Mainul Hossain, a professor at the Institute of Information Technology at the University of Dhaka, was asked whether the PHP vulnerability posed a cause for concern in Bangladesh.

“Definitely. Imagine someone taking control of the land services server and altering land records, or gaining control of the income tax website and deleting its data. What would the consequences be?” he said to Prothom Alo.

Mainul Hossain said Bangladesh needed to remain vigilant, closely monitor the measures being taken and the recommendations being issued around the world, and ensure that adequate security measures were implemented at home.

Government plans to buy vehicles for police at a cost of Tk 66.09 billion
item.description:
The government plans to spend Tk 66.09 billion to purchase 5,830 vehicles for the police force. The proposed purchases include pickup vans, SUVs for senior officers, air-conditioned buses and minibuses for transporting police personnel, and various specialised vehicles for maintaining law and order.

Police Headquarters has proposed two projects to address the force’s vehicle shortage. One involves spending Tk 43.28 billion on general operational vehicles, while the other proposes Tk 22.81 billion for specialised vehicles. The two projects together would cover the purchase of 5,830 vehicles.

The projects are scheduled to be placed for approval at a meeting of the Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (ECNEC) today, Sunday. If approved, they are expected to be completed by June 2029. These details were obtained from sources at the Ministry of Home Affairs and the Planning Commission.

Police Headquarters officials say a large number of police vehicles were burned or damaged during the 2024 student-people uprising. Many older vehicles have also broken down during operations. In addition, the force has a shortfall of vehicles against the requirements set out in its Table of Organisation and Equipment (TO&E). These factors have made the purchase of new vehicles necessary, they say.

However, officials at the Planning Commission and the Ministry of Home Affairs have expressed doubts about whether the government will be able to provide such a large amount of funding.

Tk 25.01 billion proposed for pickup vans

Under the project titled Procurement of Operational Vehicles to Enhance the Capacity of Bangladesh Police, the proposal is to purchase 4,829 vehicles at a cost of Tk 43.28 billion.

These include 2,909 double-cabin pickup vans, each priced at Tk 8.6 million. The total cost for these vehicles would be over Tk 25 billion.

The proposal also includes 400 SUVs with 2,700cc engines for senior police officers, at Tk 16.9 million each, bringing the total to Tk 6.76 billion. Another 345 jeeps with 2,000cc engines would be purchased at Tk 7.5 million each, costing approximately Tk 2.5875 billion. The two categories together account for 745 SUVs.

The project also proposes purchasing 214 microbuses at Tk 5.2 million each, for a total of Tk 1.1128 billion.

For transporting police personnel, the proposal includes non-air-conditioned large buses and air-conditioned minibuses. The draft provides for 148 non-AC buses at Tk 5.2 million each and 148 AC minibuses at Tk 12 million each. Other proposed purchases include prison vans, patrol vehicles, ambulances and speedboats.

Officials at the Ministry of Home Affairs said the prices had been set by a cost-estimation committee at Police Headquarters. The five-member committee includes four senior police officials and an assistant professor from the Department of Mechanical Engineering at Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET).

Tk 22.81 billion for specialised vehicles

The project titled Procurement of Specialised Vehicles to Enhance the Capacity of Bangladesh Police has an estimated cost of Tk 22.81 billion. It would fund the purchase of 1,001 specialised vehicles, with the stated aim of improving the police force’s efficiency and operational capacity to maintain law and order.

The proposal includes purchasing 11 armoured personnel carriers (APCs) at a cost of Tk 1.32 billion to deal with situations such as labour unrest in industrial areas.

Other proposed purchases under the project include 20 water cannons, 20 riot-control vehicles, 15 SWAT vans, 100 specialised patrol cars, 13 specialised vans, 55 prison vans and 200 motorcycles, along with other specialised vehicles.

Home Secretary Manzur Morshed Chowdhury told Prothom Alo that some specialised vehicles were also being purchased for police personnel who would serve in United Nations peacekeeping missions. The UN would reimburse the cost later, he said. He added that many police vehicles had been damaged during the uprising, which was one reason for the larger number of pickup vans being proposed.

Asked how the vehicles would be maintained after purchase, the secretary said the police had their own arrangements for vehicle maintenance.

Several officials at the Planning Commission and the Ministry of Home Affairs told Prothom Alo that they were uncertain whether the government could fund such a large expenditure over the next three years given the current state of revenue collection.

They said transparency in the procurement of such a large number of vehicles would also be crucial. A clear plan was needed for meeting the ongoing costs of fuel, repairs, spare parts, tyres, insurance and other operating expenses. For specialised vehicles, training, technical support and a reliable supply of spare parts would also need to be ensured.

item.title: Deep depression over Bay of Bengal, may develop into cyclone tomorrow
item.description:
The deep depression formed over the Bay of Bengal may turn into a cyclone by tomorrow, Monday.

Subsequently, it could evolve into a very severe cyclonic storm and is expected to cross the coast of Andhra Pradesh state in India by next Wednesday.

This information was reported in a special bulletin from the Meteorological Department on Sunday afternoon.

The bulletin states that the low-pressure area over the east-central Bay of Bengal and adjoining southeast Bay of Bengal has intensified into a deep depression.

At noon today, it was located 810 kilometers south of Chittagong seaport, 730 kilometers south of Cox's Bazar, 840 kilometers south of Mongla, and 780 kilometers south of Payra seaport.

According to the Meteorological Department's forecast, the deep depression may intensify further as it moves southwestward. It is likely to change course to the west-northwest direction later.

Within the 48 kilometers of the deep depression's centre, the maximum sustained wind speed is 50 kilometers per hour. It is increasing to 60 kilometers per hour in gusts or squalls. The sea is rough near the centre of the depression.

In this situation, Chittagong, Cox's Bazar, Mongla, and Payra seaports have been advised to hoist distant warning signal number 1.

Fishing boats and trawlers in the north Bay of Bengal are advised to remain close to the coast and proceed with caution until further notice.

Meteorologist AKM Nazmul Islam from the Meteorological Department told Prothom Alo on Sunday evening that the cyclone might cross the coast of Andhra Pradesh state, India, on Wednesday.

Due to its influence, rain may begin in several parts of the country on Tuesday. Rain is expected to spread over a larger part of the country over the following two days.

item.title: COP17 faces crunch talks over biodiversity funding, indigenous rights
item.description:
Negotiations at the UN biodiversity conference COP17 are entering a critical phase, with countries divided over who should pay for nature conservation and how Indigenous peoples and local communities should participate in decisions affecting their territories and livelihoods.
The first week of formal discussions concluded on Friday evening, with negotiations set to resume on Monday. Funding responsibilities, gender equality, human rights protections and inclusive decision-making remain among the key unresolved issues.
The conference is expected to test countries’ commitment to the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, adopted in 2022, which aims to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030.
However, a draft global progress assessment published in July and analysed by Carbon Brief found that countries were off track on 22 of the framework’s 23 targets, highlighting a significant gap between international commitments and implementation.
Guido Broekhoven, WWF’s interim global director for multilateral policy, said the first week had brought difficult decisions into focus but had yet to resolve them. He urged ministers to translate the assessment into stronger national implementation measures.
The Armenian presidency is seeking an overarching outcome, known as the “Yerevan Pathway”, to identify implementation gaps and establish priorities for measurable progress over the next two years.
Financing remains one of the most contentious issues. The European Union and several developed countries want to expand the pool of contributors to include major emerging economies and Gulf states, including China and India.
Supporters argue that the global economic landscape has changed considerably since the list of official donor countries was last reviewed in 2006. They say countries’ current economic capacity should be reflected in their contributions to biodiversity protection.
Developing countries, however, argue that established donors must first fulfil their existing financial commitments before the rules governing funding responsibilities are changed.
The distinction between voluntary contributions and formally assigned funding obligations has become a central point of contention. Saudi Arabia and Qatar have also opposed proposals to broaden the pool of official donors.
Juliette Landry, a researcher at the Institute for Sustainable Development and International Relations, said Saudi Arabia and Qatar had blocked discussions during the summer. China, meanwhile, supports developing countries but does not want to accept formal funding obligations, she said.
Under the global biodiversity framework, countries aim to mobilise at least $200 billion annually from all sources by 2030. International biodiversity finance for developing countries is expected to reach at least $20 billion a year by 2025 and $30 billion by 2030.
Carbon Brief’s analysis suggests that the 2025 financing milestone may not have been met, although further data are needed for a definitive assessment.
A high-level dialogue on the Global Biodiversity Framework Fund and an announcement of financial pledges are scheduled for October 26, followed by ministerial discussions on Tuesday and Wednesday.
Beyond the amount pledged, negotiators face another challenge: ensuring that conservation funding reaches the people protecting ecosystems on the ground.
Bangladeshi negotiator Zahidul Kabir said Bangladesh supports simplifying access to international biodiversity finance for communities dependent on nature and ensuring that funding reaches them directly.
He said supporting livelihoods that depend on natural resources could help reduce pressure on biodiversity, while civil society organisations could play an important role in working with local communities.
Kazi Amdadul Hoque of Friendship stressed the need to empower communities facing environmental pressures to participate in decision-making.
River erosion and salinity are already affecting agriculture, drinking water and daily life in vulnerable areas, underscoring the importance of locally led conservation and adaptation initiatives.
Negotiators are also discussing a commitment to reduce harmful incentives, including subsidies, by at least $500 billion annually by 2030. Any reform, however, must take into account the livelihoods of farmers, fishers and workers who depend on existing support.
Eva Zabey, executive director of Business for Nature, has argued that harmful subsidies should not be treated solely as an environmental issue, as reform also affects public finance, economic policy and competitiveness.
The slow progress of the Cali Fund has intensified concerns about the private sector’s contribution to biodiversity conservation.
The fund is designed to share benefits arising from the commercial use of digital sequence information (DSI) on genetic resources, which can support research and product development in pharmaceuticals and biotechnology.
According to The Guardian, pledges to the fund stood at $10,656 at the start of the conference, with only $7,085 paid in. The fund aims to raise $1 billion annually.
At least half of its resources are intended to support the self-identified needs of Indigenous peoples and local communities. However, questions remain over contributions, allocation rules and how benefit-sharing obligations will work in practice.
The Cali Fund is separate from the Global Biodiversity Framework Fund, which supports broader biodiversity-related priorities.
Target 22 of the Global Biodiversity Framework calls for inclusive participation in biodiversity-related decision-making, access to justice and information, and respect for the rights of Indigenous peoples and local communities. It also highlights protections for environmental human rights defenders.
Yet Carbon Brief’s assessment has identified gaps in national commitments, monitoring and reporting, including limited attention to protecting environmental defenders.
Disagreements have also emerged over wording on human rights safeguards and gender equality in forest-related negotiations. The final language could determine how explicitly these protections are reflected in implementation.
Nakeu Leshao, an Indigenous rights advocate from Kenya’s Maasai Mara, told the media that Indigenous peoples and local communities must have meaningful and distinct opportunities to participate in biodiversity decisions. Funding should reach communities directly so they can pursue their own conservation priorities, she said.
The conference is due to conclude on Friday. Ministers now face the challenge of turning the global assessment into measurable action backed by reliable financing, meaningful community participation and clear human rights safeguards.
Without progress on these issues, the ambition to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030 risks remaining far ahead of implementation.
